items.name: TCP connections and their cost
items.explanation: TCP lets two hosts open a connection and exchange data reliably. Each open connection holds some memory and bookkeeping at both ends, even when idle, which is why proxies reuse them.

assumedBy.quote: It’s common for proxies to maintain long-lived connections to the backend tasks to avoid the cost of setting up and tearing down TCP connections for every request.

items.name: The TLS handshake
items.explanation: Before an encrypted connection carries data, client and server agree on a TLS version and security settings in a handshake. It costs time and CPU, which matters when many clients reconnect at once.

assumedBy.quote: This approach puts too much memory pressure on servers, and TLS handshakes during server restarts can overwhelm servers.

sources.title: Transport Layer Security (TLS): the TLS handshake

items.name: Reverse proxies
items.explanation: A reverse proxy sits in front of servers, receives requests and passes them on. Proxying is commonly used to spread load across several servers.

assumedBy.quote: At a very high level, Uber’s service mesh architecture is centered around an on-host L7 reverse proxy

items.name: Service discovery
items.explanation: Service discovery keeps a record of where each service currently runs, so clients ask for the address instead of hard-coding it. When tasks move or fail, the record changes and clients follow.

assumedBy.quote: This system interfaces with cluster management to keep the most up-to-date information about the service backend tasks.
Our in-house service discovery system can scale to hundreds of thousands of hosts across multiple data centers around the globe.

items.name: Eventual consistency
items.explanation: Strong consistency means every read sees the latest write; eventual consistency means the copies agree after a delay.

assumedBy.quote: The eventual consistency guaranteed by ZooKeeper/etcd is good enough for service discovery as well.
